notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Georgia (Mzhavanadze). Shevardnadze's Interior Ministry in 7 (KGB under Inauri mentioned there), Georgian Stalin cult (1956 riots) as hardliners in 6. Georgian Menshevik exile party (Leuville) in 3. Abkhaz national movement in 19 as Leninist-legalist national communists. Gamsakhurdia/Kostava circle in 20. Islamic slots use real Georgian Muslim communities (Tbilisi Jumah Mosque, Borchali Azerbaijanis, Batumi Orta Jame, Upper Adjara, Meskhetian Turks). Bagrationi uses MD's GEO_nationalist_monarchist sprite.

0.name: Radio Tavisupleba
0.text:
The Georgian Service of Radio Liberty broadcasts from Munich into the Georgian SSR, funded by Washington and staffed by émigrés of the 1921 and wartime emigrations. Despite Soviet jamming, its programmes on history, religion and suppressed literature reach listeners in Tbilisi, Kutaisi and the villages.

It promotes a Western-aligned, anti-communist Georgia and recalls the independent republic of 1918–1921, though its émigré staff are divided between democrats, nationalists and conservative officers who favour a strong hand. It has no organisation inside the republic. Its leverage lies in information: every Soviet secret it airs undermines the party's monopoly on truth.

1.name: Sakartvelos mtserlta kavshiri
1.text:
The Writers' Union of Georgia is the official guild of the republic's authors and guardian of a literary tradition reaching back to Shota Rustaveli. Its ranks span the elder novelist Konstantine Gamsakhurdia, the popular prose writer Nodar Dumbadze and a younger generation of poets who treat the Georgian language almost as a sacred trust.

Loyal to Soviet power in public, the union defends the primacy of Georgian in schools and administration, the protection of churches and monuments, and a proud national history. It resists Russification and centralisation with petitions and quiet lobbying. Its leverage lies in the immense prestige of literature in Georgian society and the party's fear of offending national pride.

2.name: Sakartvelos kinematograpistta kavshiri
2.text:
The Union of Cinematographers of Georgia brings together the directors of the Georgia-Film studio, whose work has made Georgian cinema famous across the Soviet Union and at Western festivals. Tengiz Abuladze, Otar Iosseliani, Eldar and Giorgi Shengelaia and Lana Gogoberidze belong to a generation that prizes irony, poetry and individual conscience over socialist realism.

Their films test the censors with ambiguity and humour, and some, like Iosseliani's, run into trouble with Goskino. They want artistic freedom, contacts with Europe and an honest look at Georgian life, without challenging Soviet power head-on. Their leverage lies in an international prestige that Moscow is reluctant to sacrifice.

3.name: Sakartvelos sotsial-demokratiuli partia
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Georgia, the Menshevik party that governed the independent Democratic Republic of Georgia from 1918 until the Red Army invasion of 1921, survives in French exile. Its centre is the estate at Leuville-sur-Orge near Paris, where Noe Zhordania's government-in-exile sat until his death in 1953 and where the émigré community still gathers.

The party stands for democratic socialism, parliamentary government, land for the peasants and an independent Georgia within a free Europe, and keeps ties with European social democrats. Its veterans are ageing and their children assimilating. Inside Georgia its legacy is officially reviled, but family memories of 1918 keep its name alive.

4.name: Sakartvelos komunisturi partia
4.text:
The Communist Party of Georgia is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Georgian SSR. Since 1953 it has been led by First Secretary Vasil Mzhavanadze, a former army general and candidate member of the Politburo, who governs through an easy-going system of patronage that keeps the republic calm and prosperous by Soviet standards.

The party balances loyalty to Moscow with tolerance for Georgian pride, a thriving second economy and rampant corruption that reaches into Mzhavanadze's own household. It promotes tea, citrus, wine, tourism and heavy industry in Rustavi and Kutaisi. Its power rests on the nomenklatura and on Brezhnev's goodwill, which ambitious rivals are already testing.

5.name: Sakartvelos leninuri komunisturi akhalgazrda kavshiri
5.english: Leninist Young Communist League of Georgia
5.text:
The Leninist Young Communist League of Georgia is the republic's Komsomol, organising pupils, students and young workers from Tbilisi to the tea plantations of Guria. Eduard Shevardnadze led it from 1957 to 1961, and its alumni now fill the ranks of the police, the party and the ministries.

Its activist core sees itself as the conscience of the revolution, scornful of the profiteering, nepotism and lavish feasts of Mzhavanadze's Georgia and of the black-market fortunes flaunted in Tbilisi. It calls for discipline, honesty, collective labour and internationalism. Its leverage lies in mobilisation and in a ladder of promotion that links it directly to Shevardnadze's reforming network.

6.name: Stalinis ertgulni
6.text:
Stalin's Faithful are the Georgians who never accepted Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin: veterans, retired officials, Gori patriots and the young men who in March 1956 filled the streets of Tbilisi to defend his memory until troops opened fire. They keep his portrait in homes, cars and offices, and the Stalin Museum in Gori is their shrine.

They see Stalin as a great Georgian who made the USSR a superpower, and demand his rehabilitation, iron discipline, an end to corruption and a strong centralised state. Many sit in the party apparatus and among army veterans. Their leverage lies in a popular cult that no Georgian leader dares to confront openly.

7.name: Sakartvelos SSR shinagan sakmeta saministro
7.english: Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Georgian SSR
7.text:
The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Georgian SSR commands the republic's militia and has been headed since 1965 by Eduard Shevardnadze, a former Komsomol leader known for personal austerity and burning ambition. Alongside it stands the republican KGB, led since 1954 by Aleksi Inauri.

Shevardnadze's officers are building dossiers on the underground millionaires, bribe-takers and party patrons of Mzhavanadze's Georgia, waiting for Moscow's signal to strike. They favour order, discipline and a purge of the corrupt old guard, and see firmness rather than ideology as the cure for Georgia's ills. Their leverage lies in files, arrests and Shevardnadze's growing standing in Moscow.

8.name: Tiflis Cümä mäscidi
8.text:
The Tbilisi Jumah Mosque, below the Narikala fortress, is the only functioning mosque in the Georgian capital. Since the city's Shia mosque was demolished in 1951, Shia and Sunni believers pray side by side in the same hall. Its congregation is drawn mostly from the Azerbaijanis of Tbilisi and the Borchali districts, and it answers to the Spiritual Board of the Muslims of Transcaucasia in Baku.

Its akhunds preach loyalty to the state, tolerance between Muslims and Christians and the preservation of family piety. They seek little more than permission for religious instruction and respect for Muslim holidays. Their leverage rests on being the recognised voice of Georgia's largest Muslim community.

9.name: Borçalı mollaları
9.text:
The Mullahs of Borchali are the unregistered clerics of the Azerbaijani villages of Marneuli, Bolnisi and Dmanisi in southern Georgia, where the Soviet state allows almost no mosques. They lead Friday prayers in private houses, recite elegies for Imam Husayn during Muharram and conduct marriages and funerals by Shia rite.

They regard the official clergy as compromised and look to the senior clerics of Najaf and to Iranian religious literature smuggled across the Caucasus. They demand strict observance and resistance to atheist schooling and assimilation. Their leverage lies in villages where they, not the kolkhoz chairman, preside over life's great moments.

10.name: Batumis Orta Jame
10.text:
The Orta Jame Mosque of Batumi is the only mosque left open in the capital of Adjara, the autonomous republic of Muslim Georgians who lived under Ottoman rule until 1878. Its Sunni imams answer to the mufti of the Spiritual Board in Baku and minister to a community whose faith has been battered by decades of atheist campaigns and pressure to abandon 'Turkish' customs.

The mosque teaches quiet, loyal piety in the Hanafi tradition: prayer, fasting, modest family life and respect for authority. It avoids politics and stresses that Adjarians are Georgians as well as Muslims. Its leverage lies in the persistence of Islam in Adjara's mountain villages, where many families still keep the faith.

11.name: Zemo Acharis khojebi
11.text:
The Hojas of Upper Adjara are the clandestine Quran teachers of the mountain districts of Khulo and Shuakhevi, where Islam has survived Soviet repression in secret village schools. Trained by elders schooled in Ottoman madrasas before 1921, they keep Arabic learning, Ottoman books and the memory of the caliphate alive.

They regard Soviet rule as a passing trial and dream of a restored Islamic order under a caliph, as their grandfathers knew under the Ottoman sultans. Some have relatives among the Adjarian emigrants in Turkey. Their numbers are small and their activity limited to teaching and prayer, but their leverage lies in the loyalty of isolated villages that the state barely reaches.

12.name: Ahıska Yolu
12.text:
The Road to Akhaltsikhe is the movement of the Meskhetian Turks, the Muslim people of southern Georgia deported to Central Asia in November 1944. Organised through village assemblies and a committee for return formed in the 1960s, its delegates have petitioned Moscow again and again, and families who tried to resettle in Georgia have been turned back.

The movement demands rehabilitation and the right to return to Meskheti and live there as a Muslim, Turkish-speaking community with its own schools and mosques. Its methods are peaceful: petitions, congresses and appeals to Soviet law, with elders and imams lending moral weight. Its leverage lies in persistence and growing attention abroad.

13.name: Sakartvelos SSR Ministrta Sabcho
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Georgian SSR
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Georgian SSR is the republic's government, chaired since 1953 by Givi Javakhishvili, a cautious administrator who has outlasted every shift in Moscow. With the State Planning Committee it runs the Rustavi metallurgical works, the Inguri hydroelectric project, the tea and citrus economy and a booming Black Sea tourist trade.

Its technocrats judge policy by output and stability rather than ideology, bargaining quietly with Union ministries for investment and tolerating the informal economy that keeps Georgians prosperous. They avoid both national agitation and Moscow's campaigns. Their leverage lies in their grip on budgets, supplies and appointments throughout the republic's economy.

14.name: Sakartvelos martlmadidebeli eklesia
14.text:
The Georgian Orthodox Church, autocephalous since the early Middle Ages and restored as such in 1917, is led by Catholicos-Patriarch Ephrem II. Battered by Soviet persecution, it keeps only a few dozen open churches and a single seminary at Mtskheta, and its leadership is widely seen as compromised by KGB pressure and accused of corruption.

Yet it remains the symbol of Georgian nationhood, and younger hierarchs such as Metropolitan Ilia of Sukhumi and Abkhazia, rector of the Mtskheta seminary, hope to revive it. The church stands for faith, family and national tradition while avoiding confrontation with the state. Its leverage lies in a national identity inseparable from Orthodoxy.

15.name: Tbilisis milionerebi
15.text:
The Tbilisi Millionaires are the underground entrepreneurs of the second economy, who run illegal workshops inside state factories, producing fashionable clothing, raincoats and consumer goods from diverted materials. The most famous, Otar Lazishvili, is reputed to control an empire of workshops, warehouses and protected officials.

They buy posts, licences and silence from party and police patrons, and their fortunes fund feasts, cars and dachas that Tbilisi openly admires. They want the regime of easy corruption to continue and dread any anti-corruption campaign. Ideology means nothing to them; their leverage lies in cash, consumer goods and the officials whose lifestyles they finance.

16.name: Mandarinis vachrebi
16.text:
The Mandarin Traders are the Georgian peasants and middlemen who carry citrus fruit, flowers, wine and tea from private plots in Guria, Samegrelo, Adjara and Kakheti to the markets of Moscow, Leningrad and the Urals. A single season's sales can buy a car, and their prosperity is the envy of the Union.

They want freedom to grow, transport and sell without inspectors, roadblocks or campaigns against 'speculation', and see the state mainly as an obstacle to be bribed. They are indifferent to ideology and loyal to family and village. Their leverage is economic: the republic's informal prosperity rests on their trade, and few officials refuse their gifts.

17.name: Sakartvelos bunebis datsvis sazogadoeba
17.text:
The Georgian Society for Nature Conservation is the republic's official voluntary environmental body, uniting biologists, foresters, geographers and teachers under the patronage of the Academy of Sciences. Its scientists study the reserves of Lagodekhi and Borjomi and the subtropical wetlands of Kolkheti.

They warn against the erosion of the Black Sea beaches, uncontrolled logging in the mountains, pollution of the Mtkvari by Rustavi's steelworks and the ecological costs of the giant Inguri dam. They work through reports, lectures and requests for new reserves, avoiding any open challenge to the plan. Their leverage lies in scientific authority and the deep Georgian attachment to land and landscape.

18.name: Sakartvelos kolmeurneobata respublikuri sabcho
18.english: Republican Kolkhoz Council of the Georgian SSR
18.text:
The Republican Kolkhoz Council of the Georgian SSR is one of the new collective-farm councils created after the Third All-Union Congress of Collective Farmers in November 1969. It brings together chairmen of tea, citrus, grape and grain kolkhozes from Guria to Kakheti, many of them powerful patrons in their districts.

Its members want higher procurement prices for tea and grapes, autonomy from district party committees, investment in rural roads and housing, and pensions for kolkhozniks. Socialist in principle and pragmatic in practice, they protect the private plots that feed their villages. Their leverage lies in their control of land, labour and the rural patronage networks of the nomenklatura.

19.name: Apsny
19.text:
Apsny is the national movement of the Abkhaz intelligentsia and party cadres, who look back to Nestor Lakoba's Soviet Abkhazia of the 1920s, a republic of its own federated by treaty with Georgia until its downgrading in 1931. Through collective letters and mass meetings in 1957, 1964 and 1967 they have demanded protection against Georgian settlement and transfer to the Russian Federation.

The movement works within Soviet legality, invoking Leninist nationality policy against what it calls Georgian chauvinism. It seeks more Abkhaz cadres, Abkhaz-language schooling and broadcasting, and a higher status for the autonomous republic. Its leverage lies in Moscow's readiness to use Abkhaz grievances as a check on Tbilisi.

20.name: Gorgasliani
20.text:
Gorgasliani is the circle of Georgian national dissidents around Zviad Gamsakhurdia and Merab Kostava, who first organised under that name in 1954 as an underground youth group named after the fifth-century King Vakhtang Gorgasali and were arrested for anti-Soviet leaflets in the late 1950s. Gamsakhurdia now works as a literary scholar and translator, Kostava as a musicologist.

The circle denounces Russification, the decay of Georgian monuments and the corruption of the church hierarchy, and dreams of a free, Christian Georgia. It works through samizdat, petitions and personal networks among students and the intelligentsia. Its leverage lies in moral courage and in a national feeling that runs deep.

21.name: Legionerebi
21.text:
The Legionnaires are the veterans of the Georgian Legion, raised by the Wehrmacht in 1942 from Soviet prisoners of war and émigrés, who escaped repatriation in 1945 and settled in West Germany, France and the Americas. Ageing and scattered, they keep up veterans' associations, memorial services and émigré newspapers.

Their outlook mixes Georgian ultranationalism, militarism, fierce anti-communism and lingering sympathy for fascist Germany as the enemy of Moscow. They despise the democratic émigrés of Leuville and dream of a Georgia freed by force of arms. In the Soviet republic they are reviled as traitors and have no following; their leverage is limited to the émigré press and nostalgia.

22.name: Zakavkazskiy voyennyy okrug
22.text:
The Transcaucasian Military District, headquartered in Tbilisi, commands the Soviet Army in Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, facing NATO's Turkey and the Shah's Iran across the southern frontier. Its garrisons, airfields and the naval base at Poti make Tbilisi one of the Union's great military centres.

The officer corps is mostly Russian and Ukrainian, though Georgians serve in considerable numbers and Mzhavanadze himself is a lieutenant general. It distrusts nationalist unrest, remembers the shootings of March 1956 in Tbilisi and stands ready to act again. Its leverage lies in its divisions, its role as guardian of the southern border and Moscow's trust.

23.name: Bagrationta dinastia
23.text:
The House of Bagrationi ruled Georgian kingdoms for a thousand years until Russia annexed Kartli-Kakheti in 1801 and Imereti in 1810. Its senior claimant, Prince Irakli Bagration of Mukhrani, lives in Madrid with his family and presents himself as head of the royal house of Georgia.

The royalists dream of an independent Christian Georgian monarchy rooted in Orthodoxy and the national past, and reject Soviet power utterly. In the Soviet republic monarchism has no organisation, yet the Bagrationi name, carried by many ordinary families, remains woven into Georgian history. Its leverage lies in legitimacy and the romance of the medieval golden age.
